title: How do you monitor Flink jobs — Flink Web Dashboard (job graph, checkpoints, backpressure, exceptions), Flink Metrics (latency, throughput, checkpoint duration, state size) exposed to Prometheus/Grafana/Datadog, and what metrics indicate trouble (increasing checkpoint duration, growing state size, backpressure on specific operators)?
shortTitle: How do you monitor Flink jobs and what metrics indicate trouble

s1_definition.profdef: Monitoring a Flink job combines the built-in Flink Web Dashboard with the Flink metrics system exported to an external platform. The dashboard visualizes the job graph, per-operator backpressure, checkpoint history and durations, watermarks, and exceptions, giving a live interactive view. The metrics system emits numeric time series such as records-in and records-out per second for throughput, end-to-end and operator latency, checkpoint duration and size, and state size, which you push to Prometheus, Grafana, or Datadog for dashboards, historical trends, and alerting. The warning signs of a sick job are steadily increasing checkpoint duration, continuously growing state size, rising consumer lag, and sustained backpressure concentrated on a specific operator.
s1_definition.analogy: Running a Flink job at the National Bank of India is like running the payments processing line in a branch. The Web Dashboard is the live camera feed on the wall: you can see each station, whether any station has a queue forming behind it, and whether the overnight safe-backup finished on time. The metrics system is the set of sensors wired to the head-office control room, Prometheus and Grafana, recording throughput, delays, and backup times minute by minute, with alarms that page the on-call engineer when something trends the wrong way. If one station keeps forming a queue, the safe-backups take longer every night, or the stack of unprocessed slips keeps growing, those are the signs the line is in trouble and needs attention before it stalls.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Monitoring a Flink job combines the built-in Flink Web Dashboard with the Flink metrics system exported to an external platform. The dashboard visualizes the job graph, per-operator backpressure, checkpoint history and durations, watermarks, and exceptions, giving a live interactive view. The metrics system emits numeric time series such as records-in and records-out per second for throughput, end-to-end and operator latency, checkpoint duration and size, and state size, which you push to Prometheus, Grafana, or Datadog for dashboards, historical trends, and alerting. The warning signs of a sick job are steadily increasing checkpoint duration, continuously growing state size, rising consumer lag, and sustained backpressure concentrated on a specific operator.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Running a Flink job at the National Bank of India is like running the payments processing line in a branch. The Web Dashboard is the live camera feed on the wall: you can see each station, whether any station has a queue forming behind it, and whether the overnight safe-backup finished on time. The metrics system is the set of sensors wired to the head-office control room, Prometheus and Grafana, recording throughput, delays, and backup times minute by minute, with alarms that page the on-call engineer when something trends the wrong way. If one station keeps forming a queue, the safe-backups take longer every night, or the stack of unprocessed slips keeps growing, those are the signs the line is in trouble and needs attention before it stalls.

**One line to remember:** Use the Flink Web Dashboard for live inspection of the job graph, backpressure, and checkpoints, and export Flink metrics to Prometheus or Grafana for trends and alerts, watching rising checkpoint duration, growing state, lag, and operator backpressure as the key danger signs.

sections.s2_technical:
The Flink Web Dashboard, served by the JobManager, is the first stop. It shows the logical and physical job graph so you can see every operator and its parallelism, and it colors operators by backpressure status so you can instantly spot where data is piling up. It has a checkpoints tab showing each checkpoint's duration, size, alignment time, and whether it succeeded or failed, a watermarks view showing how event time is progressing per operator, and an exceptions tab with recent failures and restarts. For live firefighting the dashboard is invaluable because it is immediate and visual.

For continuous monitoring you use the metrics system. Flink exposes metrics through reporters, most commonly the Prometheus reporter, which publishes an endpoint that Prometheus scrapes, and from there Grafana builds dashboards and alerts, or you use the Datadog reporter. The key metric families are these. Throughput appears as numRecordsInPerSecond and numRecordsOutPerSecond per operator, telling you how fast data flows. Latency can be measured with latency markers for end-to-end and per-operator latency. Checkpointing exposes lastCheckpointDuration, lastCheckpointSize, and the number of completed and failed checkpoints. State size is visible per operator and via the checkpoint size. Backpressure and the related busyTimeMsPerSecond and idleTimeMsPerSecond tell you whether an operator is the bottleneck. For sources like Kafka, records-lag-max or consumer lag tells you whether you are keeping up with the input.

Interpreting these is the real skill. Steadily increasing checkpoint duration usually means state is growing or the state backend is under pressure, and if a checkpoint cannot finish before the next one starts, the job can stall or fall behind; the fix may be incremental checkpoints, more managed memory, or reducing state via time-to-live. Continuously growing state size with no plateau signals a state leak, often a keyed state that is never cleaned up, for example a timer or map entry per key that is never removed, which eventually exhausts memory or disk; the fix is state TTL or explicit cleanup. Backpressure concentrated on one operator identifies the bottleneck: the busy operator cannot keep up, so everything upstream slows; you address it by increasing that operator's parallelism, optimizing its logic, or fixing a slow external call it makes. Rising Kafka consumer lag means the job as a whole is slower than the input rate, which ties back to backpressure or insufficient parallelism. The senior nuances are these. First, alert on trends and rates of change, not just absolute values, because a slowly rising checkpoint duration is an early warning before an outage. Second, correlate metrics: backpressure plus rising lag plus a busy operator points directly at the culprit. Third, watch failed-checkpoint counts and restart counts, since frequent restarts quietly erode throughput and may indicate a flaky sink or resource limit. Fourth, keep latency markers off in extremely high-throughput jobs where they add overhead, enabling them only when investigating. Knowing which metric reveals which failure mode, and alerting on trends, is exactly what distinguishes an engineer who keeps a streaming platform healthy from one who only reacts after it has already crashed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's real-time fraud job began missing its latency targets, and the operations team needed to know, from metrics, whether the cause was a growing-state checkpoint problem or a single slow operator. This is exactly what checkpoint duration, state size, and per-operator backpressure metrics reveal.

Problem 2 — The team wanted automated alerts that fire on dangerous trends, such as checkpoint duration rising toward the checkpoint interval or state size growing without bound, rather than discovering the problem only when the job crashed. This is exactly what Prometheus-style alert rules on metric trends provide.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models a Flink metrics collector and an alerting evaluator without a cluster. We define a `MetricSnapshot` capturing per-operator throughput and backpressure plus job-wide checkpoint duration, state size, and Kafka lag at a point in time, a `MetricsCollector` that records a series of snapshots over time, and an `AlertEvaluator` that applies rules for rising checkpoint duration, growing state size, sustained operator backpressure, and increasing lag, emitting alerts exactly as a monitoring system would. A `MonitoringDemo` main class feeds a sequence of snapshots representing a degrading job and prints the health status and the alerts raised.

```
flink-monitoring-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/flink/mon/
│   │   │   ├── MonitoringDemo.java        (main runnable demo)
│   │   │   ├── MetricSnapshot.java        (one point-in-time metrics reading)
│   │   │   ├── MetricsCollector.java      (records snapshots over time)
│   │   │   └── AlertEvaluator.java        (trend rules -> alerts)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── prometheus_rules.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/flink/mon/
│           └── AlertEvaluatorTest.java
```

The Prometheus alert rules this demo models:

```yaml
# prometheus_rules.yml
groups:
- name: flink-fraud-job
  rules:
  - alert: CheckpointDurationRising
    expr: flink_jobmanager_lastCheckpointDuration > 50000   # 50s approaching interval
    for: 2m
  - alert: StateSizeGrowing
    expr: deriv(flink_taskmanager_job_task_operator_stateSize[10m]) > 0
    for: 10m
  - alert: OperatorBackpressured
    expr: flink_taskmanager_job_task_backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond > 500
    for: 1m
  - alert: KafkaConsumerLagHigh
    expr: flink_taskmanager_job_task_operator_records_lag_max > 100000
    for: 5m
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four metric snapshots taken one minute apart as the fraud job gradually degrades, with the checkpoint interval set to sixty seconds.

Step 1. The first snapshot is healthy: a five-second checkpoint, eight hundred megabytes of state, low lag, and low backpressure. The collector records it as the baseline. No alerts yet because there is nothing to compare against.

Step 2. The second snapshot shows the checkpoint rising to twelve seconds and state climbing to one thousand five hundred megabytes. Comparing to the baseline, the evaluator sees state growing, so it raises a state-growth warning, an early sign. The checkpoint is still comfortably under the interval, so no checkpoint alert yet.

Step 3. The third snapshot shows the checkpoint at thirty seconds, state at two thousand six hundred megabytes, lag at forty thousand, and the fraud operator backpressured at four hundred milliseconds per second. The evaluator raises another state-growth alert because state is still climbing, but backpressure is just under the threshold and the checkpoint is still under eighty percent of the interval, so those two do not fire yet. The trend is clearly bad.

Step 4. The fourth snapshot shows the checkpoint at fifty-two seconds, which is above eighty percent of the sixty-second interval and still rising, state at four thousand one hundred megabytes, lag at one hundred fifty thousand, and the fraud operator backpressured at seven hundred milliseconds per second. Now multiple rules fire at once: a checkpoint-duration-rising alert because it is approaching the interval, a state-growth alert, an operator-backpressure alert on the fraud operator, and a Kafka-lag alert because lag crossed the threshold and is rising.

Step 5. The demo prints the total alert count. The correlated picture, growing state, lengthening checkpoints, backpressure on the fraud operator, and rising lag, points to a single story: the fraud operator's state is leaking and it has become the bottleneck, which is exactly the kind of root-cause conclusion the metrics are designed to support before the job actually fails.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Monitoring a Flink job combines the built-in Web Dashboard with the metrics system exported to an external platform. The Web Dashboard, served by the JobManager, is my first stop for live inspection: it shows the job graph with per-operator parallelism, colors operators by backpressure so I can instantly see where data piles up, and has tabs for checkpoint history and durations, watermark progress, and recent exceptions and restarts. For continuous monitoring I configure a metrics reporter, usually the Prometheus reporter, so Prometheus scrapes Flink's metrics and Grafana builds dashboards and alerts, or I use the Datadog reporter. The metric families that matter are throughput as records-in and records-out per second, latency, checkpoint duration and size, state size, operator busy time and backpressure, and for Kafka sources the consumer lag.

The real skill is interpreting them. Steadily increasing checkpoint duration usually means state is growing or the state backend is under pressure, and if a checkpoint cannot finish before the next interval the job stalls, so I respond with incremental checkpoints, more managed memory, or reducing state. Continuously growing state with no plateau signals a state leak, typically keyed state or timers that are never cleaned up, which I fix with state time-to-live or explicit cleanup. Backpressure concentrated on one operator identifies the bottleneck, because everything upstream slows behind it, and I address it by raising that operator's parallelism, optimizing its logic, or fixing a slow external call. Rising Kafka lag means the whole job is slower than the input and ties back to those causes. The senior points I stress are to alert on trends and rates of change rather than only absolute values so I get early warning, to correlate metrics because backpressure plus rising lag plus a busy operator points straight at the culprit, to watch failed-checkpoint and restart counts since frequent restarts quietly erode throughput, and to enable latency markers only when investigating because they add overhead.

At the National Bank of India our real-time fraud job started missing latency targets, and rather than guess, I read the metrics. Over successive minutes I saw state size climbing with no plateau, checkpoint duration lengthening toward the interval, the fraud operator's backpressure rising, and Kafka lag increasing. Correlating those told a single story: the fraud operator had a keyed-state leak, so its state kept growing, which lengthened checkpoints and made that operator the bottleneck, which in turn backed up the pipeline and grew the lag. I had Prometheus alert rules on those exact trends, so the on-call engineer was paged when checkpoint duration approached the interval and when state grew for ten minutes straight, well before the job actually crashed. The fix was adding state time-to-live to clean up per-key entries, after which state plateaued, checkpoints shrank, backpressure cleared, and lag drained. Being able to name which metric reveals which failure mode, to correlate them into a root cause, and to alert on trends instead of reacting after a crash is exactly what shows I keep a production streaming platform healthy rather than just watch it fall over.
